answer:
Measure an input only if learning its true value could change the council's decision, and ranking the 14 inputs by that is cheap to do before you spend anything.

**1. Pin down the decision.**
The headline is "18% vs a 10% target," so the question is whether any plausible combination of input errors pushes the real reduction below 10%. The 8-point margin helps you. Many inputs can be badly wrong without changing the answer.

**2. Put a plausible range on each input.**
For each of the 14, write a low and high value. Use your own team's judgment, other cities' experience (London, Stockholm, Singapore, Milan, New York) and the literature. This takes days, not months. Be honest about the ranges. Estimates are often overconfident.

**3. Run a sensitivity analysis on the model you already have.**
- **One at a time:** swing each input across its range with the others held at baseline, and note the resulting reduction. If an input can't pull the result below 10% even at its worst plausible value, it's not worth measuring for this decision.
- **Then jointly:** run a Monte Carlo analysis with the ranges as distributions, including correlations between inputs. This gives you P(reduction < 10%) and a ranking of which inputs drive the uncertainty.

**4. Filter the survivors on three questions.**
- Is the input both high-impact and genuinely uncertain? An impactful input you already know well doesn't need data.
- Can better data arrive before the vote? Some inputs, like how drivers will actually respond to a new charge, can't be measured beforehand at any price. Surveys of intended behavior are weak evidence, and analogues from other cities may be your best option.
- What does measuring it cost? Some inputs, such as baseline traffic counts or exemption uptake, may be cheap to measure. Others may be the bulk of the $400k.

The formal version of this is the expected value of partial perfect information (EVPPI). It asks how much better your decision gets, in expectation, if you learn one input exactly. Compare that with the cost of collecting it. If the model says the charge clears 10% in nearly all scenarios, the value of any data is low, and $400k is hard to justify.

**5. Check the things the 14 inputs don't cover.**
- **Structural uncertainty:** the model's form (mode shift, trip suppression, rerouting, time-of-day shifts) often matters more than input precision. Better data feeding a wrong structure won't help.
- **Implementation:** exemptions, enforcement, and the final price and boundary can swing outcomes more than any measured input.
- **Definitions:** make sure "18% fewer downtown car trips" matches how the council will measure the 10% target.

**6. Consider alternatives to a full $400k package.**
- Buy only the top 2–4 inputs, probably at a fraction of the price.
- Stage it: measure the cheapest high-value input first and re-run the model before deciding on the rest.
- Pair the vote with a post-launch monitoring plan and an adjustable price. If the charge can be tuned after launch, precision before the vote matters less.

**One caveat.**
Data can serve credibility as well as accuracy. If the council or public won't trust a model built on estimates, some measurement may be worth it even when it wouldn't change your own recommendation. Keep that reason separate from the decision-value analysis, so you know which one you're paying for.

If you share the model's inputs and your best low/base/high values, I can set up the tornado and Monte Carlo analysis and show you which few inputs matter.
